prize_parts.citation: for the development of sequencing by synthesis with reversibly terminated fluorescent nucleotides on clustered single molecules, enabling massively parallel DNA sequencing

statement.case_for: Massively parallel sequencing by synthesis is a simple, chemistry-driven idea that became a genuine game-changer: reversible terminator nucleotides with cleavable fluorophores, read out on clustered single molecules, cut the cost of reading DNA by orders of magnitude and reshaped biology and medicine. The consequences are fully realized and independently confirmed over some twenty years, so the maturity test I apply is met. It is also a candidate that all four members who ranked it (myself, Linke, Aili and Chabes) place in their top five, and where a two-person attribution (Balasubramanian and Klenerman, who conceived and developed the Solexa chemistry in Cambridge) is clean and defensible within the three-person cap.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that sequencing is a technology whose impact lies mainly in biology and medicine, so some will see it as a physiology or medicine prize or as a platform-engineering achievement. Attribution is also contested: Rothberg's 454 pyrosequencing was the first commercial massively parallel system, Mayer and Ju contributed clustering and terminator chemistry, and priority among Solexa, Lynx and 454 rests partly on my recollection and is not verified in the files. Choosing the Cambridge pair excludes colleagues that others regard as essential.

responses.point: Linke ranks nanopore sequencing first for its clean physical principle of ionic current blockade and its unforeseen capability of portable long-read sequencing, and ranks sequencing by synthesis second with Rothberg added as third laureate.
responses.response: I respect the elegance of nanopores, but I weigh them below sequencing by synthesis because the credit is spread over five people with real priority problems and at least one deceased pioneer, which makes a three-person attribution much harder than the Cambridge pair. On Rothberg, 454 was commercially first, but pyrosequencing chemistry was not the route that came to dominate; I would keep the prize centred on the chemistry that did, and I do not think adding a third name is needed to make it defensible. I am open to nanopores as a later separate prize.

responses.point: Chabes places protein degradation first and sequencing fifth, arguing that reversible-terminator chemistry and polymerase engineering are the decisive invention in sequencing, while noting contested overlapping commercial and patent claims and suggesting Mayer as third name.
responses.response: I agree with you that the reversible-terminator chemistry is the decisive invention, which is why I want a chemistry-focused two-name configuration. I disagree that patent overlap should push us toward adding Mayer: commercial priority is not the same as the scientific contribution of clustered single-molecule sequencing by synthesis. On your first-ranked candidate, I accept the PROTAC mechanism is convincing, but with no approved degrader drug and the credit split between PROTACs and cereblon glues across eight names, I think it fails my game-changer-with-realized-consequences test for now.

responses.point: Aili ranks base editing first with Liu, Kondo and Nishida, stressing that it is a chemical solution to a biological problem that is already clinical, and ranks sequencing fourth including Rothberg.
responses.response: Base editing is a strong, novel step and I rank it fourth myself, but I would not give it precedence over sequencing yet: it follows the 2020 CRISPR prize closely, long-term clinical safety is open, and the Kondo and Nishida question makes the attribution less clean than you suggest. I also would not carry Kondo and Nishida into a prize without verifying priority, and trainee credit for Komor and Gaudelli is a separate difficulty. Sequencing, by contrast, has a two decade record and no timing problem.

responses.point: Zou ranks molecular sieves first and halide perovskites second, accepting that perovskite efficiency is confirmed but that long-term stability, lead toxicity and scale-up are unproven, which makes recognition arguably slightly early.
responses.response: I share your second-place ranking of perovskites and your honest reading of the stability problem, which is exactly why I place them behind sequencing despite my enthusiasm for new materials in the spirit of the MOF prize. Six credited names with disputed priority among Miyasaka, Park, Snaith, Grätzel and Seok makes this a prize where we may get the allocation wrong, and I would want more evidence of durability before putting it first.

uncertainties: Exact historical priority among Solexa, Lynx and 454 and the role of Mayer and Ju is taken from recollection and cannot be verified from the files
Whether the committee views sequencing as a chemistry achievement rather than one for physiology or medicine
Whether Rothberg or a nanopore prize should be linked to sequencing, which would require dropping or restructuring names under the three-person cap
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B011 or the alternatives B005 and B012; my Warshel EVB and Uppsala ribosome connections do not relate to the shortlisted candidates.
